assertions.text: Output contains a @TableTest annotation
Multiple @TableTest methods are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing item operations, coupon logic, total calculation, and checkout.
Each @TableTest has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns.

Item operations (add/remove), coupon application (validity and replacement), cart total calculation (coupon type effects on price), and checkout (stock verification) are in separate @TableTest methods.

Each table row is independently executable — no row depends on a prior row's result. The table expresses rules, not a sequential test script. Each row specifies its own preconditions (e.g. 'Cart with items' as an input column, not implied from a previous row).
Coupon application table uses before/after columns (e.g. 'Active coupon' / 'Active coupon after?') to specify the state change when entering, replacing, or entering invalid coupon codes.

Coupon application table tests validity and replacement (valid code, expired code, nonexistent code, replacing active coupon) — not coupon type effects on price. Coupon type effects belong in the cart total table.
Table has a scenario/description column as the leftmost column
At least one output column name ends with '?' (e.g. 'Message?', 'Total?', 'Active coupon after?')
Scenario names describe conditions ('Add to empty cart', 'Replace active coupon with expired') — not outcomes ('Error', 'Success').
Column names use domain/business language (e.g. 'Product', 'Quantity', 'Message?', 'Cart total?') — not code identifiers like 'productId', 'result'.
Test method body contains no if or switch statements
Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName (if present), @Description (if present), @TableTest — not any other order.
Test method has either a @DisplayName annotation or a method name that reads as a clear, descriptive title when converted from camelCase/snake_case.
If @Description is present and the text is longer than a single short line, it uses a text block (triple-quoted string """), not string concatenation with +. Passes if @Description is absent.
Each @TableTest method has a single, uniform assertion pattern applied to all rows — not different assertions per scenario.

Product prices and coupon rules (type, amount, expiry status) are visible in the table via columns, @Description, or explicit setup — not silently hardcoded. The reader can trace how inputs lead to outputs.

TypeConverter methods are used to convert map/string table values into domain objects (e.g. Map → Cart, Map → InventoryService, map → Coupon). Test method bodies contain only arrange-act-assert — no object construction from raw table values.
Coupon data uses a single map column (e.g. [type: PERCENTAGE, value: 10]) with a @TypeConverter, rather than separate sparse columns for coupon type, value, and target product.

@Description annotations do not repeat information that the scenario names already convey. Coupon type behavior (what PERCENTAGE/FIXED/PRODUCT mean) should be expressed through descriptive scenario names, not duplicated in the description.
